claims.summary: An AFTER INSERT trigger can implement post-insert work on an eligible base table, but SQL Server does not allow AFTER triggers on views. This plan cannot install the required view translation path.

An INSTEAD OF trigger is the appropriate view mechanism, but the product explicitly prohibits adding it to an updatable view with CHECK OPTION. Keeping that clause makes the proposed deployment invalid.

An unchecked filtered view can present only branch 7 rows while still allowing a modification path that admits other values. The trigger overrides ordinary insertion, so relying only on presentation filtering does not preserve the required all-row admission check.

Removing CHECK OPTION resolves the documented incompatibility. Explicitly validating the translated inserted rowset for branch 7 before base writes preserves the original rule, including multirow input, while the base table's constraints still apply.

The product explicitly rejects adding INSTEAD OF to an updatable view while WITH CHECK OPTION remains specified. INSTEAD OF is the right replacement mechanism only after resolving that clause incompatibility; the proposed deployment keeps the conflicting condition.

This removes the enforced post-modification criterion and then writes translated values to base rows through replacement logic. claims.summary: Adding inserted sums is appropriate for an insert-only rollup when no prior contributions exist. An UPDATE also has deleted prior amounts, so this method would leave old contributions counted and produce 115 rather than 65 for invoice 1.

The UPDATE transition rowsets contain all old and new detail values. Treating new amounts as positive and old amounts as negative yields -35 for invoice 1 and +40 for invoice 2, including parents present on only one side before grouping.
An inner join of per-parent sums can work only when every affected parent occurs on both sides. Invoice 2 has no deleted group, so it is omitted despite needing the inserted 40-unit contribution.

A single scalar before/after pair might be enough under a genuinely guaranteed single-row update, but this statement changes multiple details and parents. DML triggers receive rowsets, so selecting one pair discards necessary contributions.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: The actual article establishes statement-level activation, old/new logical rowsets, AFTER following successful statement and constraint processing, and triggers executing within transactions. The unit explicitly identifies deleted as old and inserted as new values for UPDATE and demonstrates rowset-based pairing. Its introductory inventory UPDATE has no grouping and is not evidence of correctness for many details sharing a parent. I instead re-derived both invoice deltas from the supplied complete transition data. The programmability module actually links this unit.

SELECT's query-expression grammar admits UNION ALL, and its SUM/GROUP BY example explicitly produces one summed row per group. Combined with the transition-table contract and the provided numbers, this supports per-parent net aggregation rather than dropping a parent absent from one side. The actual window training SELECT/WHERE reference establishes its direct preparation ancestry; no doc-to-doc approval is used.

choiceReviews.rationale: Inserted has (invoice 2,40) and (invoice 1,15), while deleted has both old invoice-1 amounts 30 and 20. Adding only inserted sums yields invoice 1 = 115 and invoice 2 = 90, so it retains the replaced old contributions. It is appropriate for an insert-only delta, not this UPDATE.

Signed transition rows give invoice 1 contributions +15,-30,-20, summing to -35, and invoice 2 contribution +40. Grouping that combined rowset once per parent yields 100-35 = 65 and 50+40 = 90. It does not require each parent to occur in both transition tables, and UNION ALL does not intentionally remove contributions.

The old sums have only invoice 1, while new sums have invoices 1 and 2. Requiring a matching parent on both sides omits invoice 2 and its +40 contribution; its total stays 50 instead of 90. The strategy can work in a different update where every affected parent occurs in both sets, which the transfer deliberately violates.

One pair and one header cannot represent the two changed details and both invoice destinations. Even selecting the moved detail needs removal from one header and addition to another, while the second detail adds another delta. A scalar approach needs a genuinely restricted single-parent/single-row problem, not this rowset.
